description:
Our team is building a tool using NASA data to find Earth locations that resemble the Moon and Mars. It will compare deserts, rocky areas, and cold regions, map the best matches, and identify potential sites in Pakistan.

No expertise needed—just curiosity and a desire to build something real!

Useful skills: Python, data analysis, app design, communication, or an interest in space and geography.
summary:
🎯 The Problem

Finding places on Earth that have environmental and geographical conditions similar to the Moon and Mars is challenging.

    🌡️ Different planetary environments have different temperature conditions.
    💧 Rainfall and humidity affect the characteristics of Earth locations.
    🏔️ Terrain features such as slope and elevation also matter.
    🔍 Comparing many locations and environmental factors manually takes time.

Our goal is to make these comparisons easier through one interactive platform.
💡 Our Solution

We developed Earth Analogue Explorer to help users explore and compare selected Earth locations with Moon and Mars conditions.

    📍 Evaluate 35 selected Earth locations.
    🌍 Explore locations through an interactive 3D globe.
    📊 Compare environmental and terrain characteristics.
    🧮 Calculate similarity percentages using our Planetary Analog Similarity Model (PASM).
    ⚖️ Adjust environmental weights to explore different comparison results.
details:
How it works. The user picks a target, either Mars (Jezero Crater) or the Moon (South Pole). The app then scores candidate sites by how closely their conditions match that target. For Pakistan, which is our home-region focus, and for a set of world sites, we pull climate data from NASA POWER, including temperature, solar radiation and related variables. We also pull terrain slope and relief from ASTER elevation data. Each site gets a similarity score against the target body. The results appear on an interactive Plotly map, and users can compare and rank sites. To keep the app fast, we fetch the NASA data once, store it in a backend CSV and load it from there. This means we don’t make live API calls on every visit.

Benefits. Analog research is usually limited to a few well-known sites, such as the Atacama Desert and Utah. Our tool shows that other regions, including Pakistan’s deserts, high-altitude terrain and cold, dry areas, can also serve as useful analogs. It brings together climate and terrain data in one place, so users don’t have to search several datasets by hand. It is also reproducible, because every score comes from open NASA data. Local researchers, universities and space-education programs get a low-cost way to explore analog science.

Intended impact. We want to make analog-site discovery more accessible and to put underrepresented regions on the map for space research. Pakistan has a growing space-science community, and we hope this tool supports student research, mission-concept studies and public outreach. Because the method works with any location’s data, it can be extended to any country.

Tools and technologies. Python, Streamlit for the app interface, Plotly for the interactive maps and charts, Pandas and NumPy for data processing, the NASA POWER API for climate data, and ASTER elevation data for terrain slope and relief. No special hardware is needed, since everything runs in the browser.

Creativity. Our approach treats analog-finding as a similarity-scoring problem across several datasets, instead of a one-off literature search. Putting Earth, Moon and Mars comparisons into one map-based tool is new for a student project. We also focus on regions that are usually overlooked, which gives the project a local identity as well as a global use.

Factors we considered. Data reliability and open access, so we used only public NASA sources. Performance, so we cache data instead of calling the API live. Scientific fairness, because climate alone doesn’t define a good analog, so we added terrain data. Usability, so that non-experts can use the app without training. Scalability, so that more sites and variables can be added later. Our team of three divided the work across data collection, scoring logic and visualization and presentation.
